# Exact inertia of the physical canonical-simplex cap Hessian

Fix d>=2 and m=d+1. Use barycentric coordinates lambda in R^m with
sum_i lambda_i=1, and let the reference simplex have vertices e_i.
Give its affine span any fixed Euclidean metric; its d-volume is V>0.
Fix the m closed caps lambda_i>=1/m. Each has volume Gamma V, where
Gamma=(d/m)^d. These caps cover the entire affine span, since some
barycentric coordinate is at least1/m.

A nearby labeled simplex has vertices the columns of W, where each
column sum is one and W is close to I. Put W=I+tB, with each column
sum of B zero. This is a physical motion of vertices, not a change
of the fixed cap inequalities. All volumes are smooth near I, where
each cap contains precisely its corresponding vertex.

## 1. Exact volume and cap formulas

The simplex volume is V det W near I. To justify the determinant,
W preserves the sum-of-coordinates functional, its induced map on
the one-dimensional quotient by the direction hyperplane is identity,
and its determinant on that direction hyperplane is det W. The
orientation remains positive near I.

Write h=d/m. The i-th cap volume is

    F_i(W)=V det W (W_ii-1/m)^d /
                     product_(j!=i)(W_ii-W_ij).       (1)

Indeed the retained cap is a simplex at vertex i, and its ratios on
the d incident edges are (W_ii-1/m)/(W_ii-W_ij). All denominators are
positive in the chosen neighborhood. Define

    L(W)=V det W - [1/(m Gamma)] sum_i F_i(W).         (2)

If T=tr B and R_i=sum_j B_ij, differentiating(1) at I gives

    F_i'(0)/(Gamma V)=T+R_i.

Since sum_i R_i=0, the first derivative of L is zero in every allowed
vertex direction. The multiplier1/(m Gamma) is positive and normalizes
the objective coefficient to one.

## 2. A directed-matrix formula for the Hessian

Let A be the off-diagonal part of B, with A_ii=0. Write c_j=sum_i A_ij
for its column sums and s_i=sum_j A_ij for its row sums. The column
constraint on B says B_ii=-c_i, so A determines every allowed motion.

The exact second variation of(2), divided by V, is

    Q(A)=||c||^2/d - (||s||^2+||A||_F^2)/m.           (3)

Here is a direct calculation. Put b_i=B_ii. Log differentiation gives

    (log F_i)''=-tr(B^2)-m^2 b_i^2/d
                         +sum_(j!=i)(b_i-B_ij)^2.

The square of the first log derivative is(T+R_i)^2. Average over i
and subtract from(det W)''=T^2-tr(B^2). Terms involving T cancel,
leaving

    Q= -||R||^2/m +(m/d)||b||^2
                        -(1/m)sum_(i!=j)(b_i-A_ij)^2.

Since R_i=b_i+s_i, expansion reduces this to

    Q=||b||^2/d-(||s||^2+||A||_F^2)/m,

which is(3). No second-order approximation to a cut simplex has been
substituted for its exact physical volume formula.

## 3. Complete inertia: d positive, one zero, d^2-1 negative

For a prescribed column-sum vector c, minimize

    J(A)=||s||^2+||A||_F^2

over zero-diagonal matrices having those column sums. This strictly
convex quadratic has a unique minimizer. Its stationarity equations
are

    A_ij+s_i=eta_j for i!=j.                          (4)

They are also sufficient: for any perturbation E with zero column
sums and zero diagonal, the first variation of J is
2 sum_(i!=j) eta_j E_ij=0, and its second variation is strictly
positive unless E=0.

Decompose c=cbar*1+c0, with sum_i c0_i=0. For the constant part the
minimizer is A_ij=cbar/d for i!=j, with row sums cbar. Its value
in(3) is zero. For the zero-sum part the minimizer is

    A_ij=(m c0_j+c0_i)/(dm-1), i!=j,
    s_i=-c0_i/(dm-1).                                (5)

The column sums are c0 because dm c0_j plus the sum of the other
c0_i is(dm-1)c0_j. Equations(4) hold with
eta_j=m c0_j/(dm-1), proving minimality directly. Calculation gives

    J(A)=m||c0||^2/(dm-1),
    Q(A)=(d^2-1)||c0||^2/[d(dm-1)]>0                (6)

when c0 is nonzero.

The two minimizing lifts are orthogonal for J: the zero-sum lift
has total matrix sum and total row sum zero, while the constant lift
is constant off its diagonal and in its row sums. They are also
orthogonal in the column-sum term of(3).

Every matrix A is its minimizing lift plus a unique zero-column-sum
matrix E. Equation(4) shows these two parts are J-orthogonal. The
column term in(3) is unchanged by E, so

    Q(A)=Q(minimizing lift)
                  -(||row(E)||^2+||E||_F^2)/m.       (7)

The latter term is strictly negative unless E=0. The space of c0 has
dimension m-1=d. The constant lift has dimension one. The off-diagonal
matrix space has dimension dm, and the column map is onto R^m;
therefore its kernel has dimension dm-m=m(d-1)=d^2-1. Equations(6)-(7)
prove the exact inertia claimed in the title, with no omitted modes.

## 4. What this says about shared cap constraints

For N independently variable identical reference simplices, with each
of the same m cap budgets imposed on their TOTAL cap volumes, the
aggregate Lagrangian Hessian has positive index dN. The aggregate
critical tangent is the kernel of m linear first cap derivatives.
Its intersection with a positive subspace therefore has dimension
at least dN-m. For N>=2 and d>=2 this number is positive.

The derivative map onto these m cap constraints is surjective. For one
simplex, scalar B on the direction hyperplane gives a nonzero common
derivative in all cap rows, while translations give every zero-sum
row derivative. Equivalently the formulas T+R_i display these two
subspaces directly. Thus, for a positive critical velocity, one can
choose a physical second acceleration so that each cap has second
derivative -epsilon. The objective's second derivative then equals
the strictly positive Lagrangian second derivative minus
epsilon/Gamma, and stays positive for sufficiently small epsilon>0.
The polynomial vertex path with that acceleration has strictly smaller
cap volumes and larger total volume for all sufficiently small positive
times. Smoothness of(1) and the strictly signed second derivatives
justify this statement, including all original fixed budgets.

This conclusion applies only when the chosen vertex motions are allowed
by the actual fiber compatibility constraints. Adjacent exposed source
fibers impose no such coupling. A strict containment condition can also
permit a specified pair of interior motions, as in the separately proved
three-fiber construction. At a general mixed-body extremum, active
Minkowski inclusions may forbid these directions. No rank estimate that
discards those active compatibility constraints is asserted.

The Hessian is a local physical-variation result. It does not classify
general extremizers, show that arbitrary fibers are simplices, or imply
the OC constant without additional arguments.
